analysis.one_liner: Requires car and light truck makers to raise fuel economy 20% by 1995 and 60% after 2000.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 1990 with 24 cosponsors, the bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set rising fuel economy requirements for passenger cars and, for the first time, strict standards for light trucks, using each manufacturer's 1988 fuel economy as a baseline: a 20% improvement for model years 1995-2000 and a 60% improvement from 2001 on, with caps of 45-50 mpg for cars and 35-40 mpg for light trucks. It also required more realistic fuel economy testing (colder temperatures, faster highway speeds), window labels showing the specific vehicle's fuel economy, an annual EPA study of how well official test numbers match real-world driving, and doubled fines for manufacturers that repeatedly miss the standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save money on gasoline over the life of their vehicles; the bill's findings cite prior efficiency gains that saved drivers close to $30 billion. It would also reduce U.S. oil consumption and carbon dioxide emissions, and give buyers more accurate fuel economy information through revised testing and window labels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and anyone affected by oil use

how_it_helps.text: Sets each manufacturer's car and light truck fuel economy target at its 1988 average plus 20% for model years 1995-2000 (capped at 45 mpg for cars, 35 mpg for light trucks) and plus 60% from 2001 onward (capped at 50 mpg and 40 mpg)

The bill's findings state that past fuel efficiency improvements between 1973 and 1987 saved drivers close to $30 billion, and that a 20% efficiency gain by 1995 and 60% by 2001 would save 3.3 million barrels of oil per day by 2005

Requires fuel economy testing at 50 degrees Fahrenheit with a faster highway cycle so the window sticker numbers better reflect real driving, and directs the EPA to study annually how official test results compare to cars driven by average drivers

Doubles civil penalties against manufacturers that violate the fuel economy standard three years in a row, and requires window labels showing the specific vehicle configuration's fuel economy when it falls below the manufacturer's standard

analysis.who_pays: Automobile manufacturers, which would have to redesign vehicles to meet rising fuel economy targets and face doubled fines for repeated violations. Some of that cost could reach buyers through higher vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: Higher fuel economy standards impose redesign costs on manufacturers, some portion of which can reach buyers through higher vehicle prices; the bill itself requires the Transportation Secretary to weigh the economic impact on manufacturers and consumers before setting standards for 2002-2006
Stricter standards can involve trade-offs in vehicle utility or performance, which the bill requires the Secretary to consider, along with any effects on competition and foreign trade

The standards are pegged to each manufacturer's own 1988 fuel economy, so makers that were already efficient in 1988 would have to improve from a higher baseline, an equity concern the bill does not directly address

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for drivers — lower gasoline bills over the life of a vehicle, plus reduced oil dependence and carbon emissions — is large and backed by the bill's own findings about past efficiency gains. The costs fall on manufacturers and potentially on new-car buyers, and the bill builds in safeguards (phase-ins, caps, a National Academy of Sciences review before standards for 2002-2006). The design is reasonably careful; the main honest objection is compliance cost and possible trade-offs in vehicle utility, which the bill acknowledges but does not eliminate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Boxer, with Reps. Stark and Schneider, introduced the Motor Vehicle Fuel Efficiency Act of 1990 on April 18, 1990
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on April 27, 1990 it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power
No further action was taken; there is no record of a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automobile manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they avoided rising fuel economy requirements for cars and, for the first time, light trucks, along with doubled fines for repeat violations. Drivers gained nothing from the bill's promised fuel savings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers avoided higher fuel economy mandates

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; the 24 cosponsors were mostly Democrats but included 3 Republicans, and the bill died in committee without a party-line roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have required each maker to lift fuel economy 20% by 1995-2000 and 60% after 2000, with strict light-truck standards for the first time and doubled fines for repeat violations. Light trucks were about a third of new vehicle sales and a growing profit source, so the bill's death preserved the existing 27.5 mpg car standard and left light trucks loosely regulated.
The bill projected saving 3.3 million barrels of oil per day by 2005, which would have cut gasoline demand. Its failure left petroleum consumption in the vehicle fleet untouched by new standards.
